Pitchfork (100): Called it a “watershed moment” in ’80s rock, chronicling the vices of Los Angeles with Axl Rose’s “lye-voiced” delivery and a “legendary, switchblade-sharp” band Album of The Year.

AllMusic (100): Praised it as a “turning point for hard rock” — “dirty, dangerous, and mean” in an era when heavy metal meant “nothing but a good time” Album of The Year.

SPIN (100): Compared it to the Stones and Aerosmith, calling it “the meanest slinkiest blues since The Rolling Stones didn’t suck” Album of The Year.

Rolling Stone (100): Linked its themes of sex and violence to mid-’70s rock, “jacked up with punk raunch” Album of The Year.

Entertainment Weekly (100): Found the album’s hard-rock platitudes “fresh and relevant” Album of The Year.

Classic Rock (100): Declared it “one of the greatest records of all-time” and the best-selling debut album ever Album of The Year.

Sputnikmusic (40): Criticized most tracks as generic and unimpressive compared to a band’s later work Album of The Year.
The album debuted at No. 182 on the Billboard 200 and barely sold 200,000 copies in its first six months classicrockartists.com.

Many in the mainstream press were ambivalent, with some calling it “dirty, dangerous, and mean” but lacking polish Album of The Year.

MTV’s decision to air the Welcome to the Jungle video was pivotal — it lit the fuse that turned the album into a cultural phenomenon classicrockartists.com.
While 1987 reviews were split, the album’s touring success, MTV exposure, and hit singles (Welcome to the Jungle, Sweet Child o’ Mine, Paradise City) turned it into a commercial juggernaut. By 1988, it had hit No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and was certified 18× platinum Wikipedia. Retrospectively, it’s now regarded as one of the most important and influential rock albums of all time.

Period reviews in 1987 were polarized — some hailed it as a raw, genre-shattering debut, others dismissed it as overhyped and unpolished. But the combination of MTV, touring, and hit singles quickly overrode early skepticism, cementing its place as a rock landmark.

A musical hook is a catchy part of a song that grabs your ear and stays in your head. People use many different words to describe it based on its style, sound, or role in the music. [1, 2, 3]  
Common Names for a Hook • Earworm: A tune that gets stuck in your head and loops over and over. • Catchphrase: A repeated vocal line or slogan in the lyrics. • Tag: A short phrase added at the end of a musical section. • Lick: A short, catchy solo or melodic fragment, often played on a guitar. • Riff: A repeated chord progression or melodic pattern, common in rock and pop. • Motif: A short musical idea or theme that repeats throughout a piece. • Stinger: A sharp, sudden musical accent used for emphasis.
